newsitem.title: USA: Dean Witter, Morgan Stanley holders approve merger.
newsitem.headline: Dean Witter, Morgan Stanley holders approve merger.

text.p: With shareholder approvals now in hand, Morgan Stanley Group Inc. and Dean Witter Discover & Co. are just days and some paperwork away from completing their $10.6 billion merger.

The deal, due to close this weekend after shareholders of both companies voted Wednesday to approve the merger, will create the nation's biggest securities firm in terms of market worth and dramatically realign the Wall Street hierarchy.

Dean Witter said the merger was approved by holders representing about 87 percent of its outstanding common shares. Morgan Stanley said holders representing 83 percent of shares entitled to vote approved the deal.

Still ahead for the two firms is the task of melding their operations and overcoming the cultural gaps between Morgan Stanley's blue-blooded investment banking business and Dean Witter's focus on the more blue-collar business of selling stocks and other investments to consumers.
The outcome of those efforts will be the true test of whether the combination represents a true threat to topple Merrill Lynch and Co. Inc. as industry leader.
"The hard work is still ahead in terms of integrating the firms," said Brown Brothers Harriman analyst Raphael Soifer. "In that respect, Merrill Lynch has a 20-year head start."
Dean Witter Chairman Philip Purcell was upbeat about the post-merger outlook.
At the company's annual shareholder meeting in Jersey City Wednesday, Purcell said early integration efforts had gone "exceptionally well" and expressed optimism about the merger.
"We've positioned this company so that it has a marvellous chance to win," Purcell said in a brief question and answer session after the meeting.
In the three months since the two companies announced their deal, Wall Street's landscape has continued to shift.
Among the deals announced since then, Bankers Trust New York Corp. announced it would acquire Alex. Brown Inc. and Swiss Bank Corp. reached a deal to buy Dillon Read & Co.
The Swiss Bank-Dillon Read pact came just a day after talks between Dillon Read and Dutch financial services firm Internationale Nederlanden Groep NV broke down.
For every deal that has come to fruition, a dozen are reported or rumoured in the discussion stage, involving just about every firm except Merrill Lynch, Morgan Stanley or Dean Witter.
Adding fuel to the rumour mill is the sense that the days when firms could slowly and quietly mull their alternatives are over, in large part because of the Morgan Stanley-Dean Witter deal.
"It certainly woke people up," Soifer said. "It made many, if not most, of the firms take a look at their options."
